video_title: The U.S. Builds the Smartest AI. China Is Doing Something Else.
transcript: ﻿Four days after we filmed this episode,  NVIDIA’s CEO Jensen Huang admitted to   an affair with a woman US intelligence  reportedly believes is a Chinese spy.   According to the New York Times, US  officials believe she was recruited   to gather information and potentially push  for NVIDIA’s best chips to be sold to China.   If anything, this news shows just how much  China wants American chips. Here’s the episode.   In December 2024, all of the world’s  most advanced AI companies were in the   US. A month later, DeepSeek, a Chinese  company most people had never heard of,   seemed to blow that apart by releasing an AI  model that rivalled the best ones in the US.   They claimed to have trained it for just $6  million. Meanwhile, American companies were   spending tens of millions to train their models. Marc Andreessen called it AI’s Sputnik moment.   NVIDIA lost almost $600 billion in value in  one day — the biggest one-day loss in US stock   market history. Suddenly,   everyone was saying: China had caught up. They were only half right. Almost two years later,   its models are still about six months behind the  best American ones. Still, six months isn’t that   long — especially when you consider that the US  has roughly 16 times China’s AI computing power.   So how are Chinese models this good? If you think the US can’t slow AI down   because China will catch up, this might change  your mind. Because China is keeping up. But it   couldn’t do that without American help. To understand how, it helps to start with   who’s actually building China’s AI. There are two kinds of players: tech   giants like Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance, the  company behind TikTok; and a handful of startups,   like DeepSeek and Zhipu. These companies are inventive.   DeepSeek’s model was revolutionary for  squeezing more out of fewer chips.   They’re also talented. More than half  of the world’s top AI researchers did   their undergraduate degrees in China. And more  and more of them are staying there to work.   And they do one big thing differently to US  companies: most of them open source their   best models. Anyone can download them and build  on them for free, which has made Chinese models   popular everywhere — including in the US. But it’s very hard to make money that way.   China’s six leading AI companies collectively  earn about 10% of what OpenAI and Anthropic do.   And while they’re big at home, they’re  still small next to the leading American   companies. ByteDance’s chatbot has about 380  million monthly users. ChatGPT has more than   twice as many every week. And they have  far less computing power to build with.   So China’s AI industry is inventive and  talented, but also comparatively small,   poor, and starved for chips. And yet,  its best models are surprisingly good.   Across dozens of AI tests, China’s  best models score about as well as   American models scored six and a half months ago. Earlier this year, Anthropic built Claude Mythos,   the first AI model to raise serious national  security concerns. China is expected to have   a model just as good within months. So  whatever worries you have about the most   powerful American AI today, expect it  from China about six months later.   A lot of people, myself included, think  we need to make sure these systems are   safe before we build even more powerful  ones — even if that means slowing down.   But others argue the US can’t afford  to slow down, because China won’t. And   if the US did slow down and China didn’t,  history’s most powerful technology could   be built by an authoritarian government. The White House’s AI plan is literally called   “Winning the Race.” David Sacks, Trump’s  former AI czar, put the logic simply:   the US is “only six to nine months ahead  of China. So really, every month counts.”   If every month counts, it’s worth  understanding what’s causing this gap:   what’s holding China back, and what’s  letting it build such good models anyways.   Let’s start with what holds China  back. A lot of it comes down to chips.   AI runs on lots of specialised computer chips.  Companies need them to build better models,   and then to run those models for millions of  users. More chips means you can do more of both.   The best AI chips need two things China struggles  to get. First: the machines that make them. Only   one company in the world builds the most advanced  ones: ASML, in the Netherlands. And since 2019,   starting under the first Trump administration,  the US and Dutch governments have blocked selling   them to China. China can make decent chips, with  less advanced machines — just not the best ones.   The second thing China struggles to get is memory.  AI chips need a special kind of very fast memory,   and China can’t make enough of it. And since  December 2024, US rules have banned selling   it to China too. So even Huawei, China’s leading  chip designer, only used Chinese-made memory in   about 16% of this year’s AI chips. The rest rely  on stockpiles, smuggling, or slower substitutes.   Add it all up, and the US makes about 50 times as  much AI computing power as China. That’s largely   because of American export controls. After DeepSeek, plenty of people said   the export controls had failed,  including NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.   But where they’re actually enforced, they do  hold China back. In fact, they’re one of the   few things that have actually bought the US time. And yet, China still has a lot of computing power.   So where is it all coming from?  Mostly, it’s coming from the US.   By the end of next year, about two-thirds  of Chinese AI computing power will come from   American chips. They get them three ways. Some are bought legally. In January,   the US approved sales of one of NVIDIA’s top  chips, the H200, to China — though Beijing told   its AI companies to hold off, to protect its own  chip industry. Chinese firms still needed chips,   though. So they found another route. This year,  they bought more than a million NVIDIA graphics   cards — the kind that are normally used for  gaming and design, which fall just under the   export rules’ limits — to use on AI. Some chips are smuggled. In one case,   smugglers peeled the NVIDIA labels off top AI  chips and replaced them with a made-up brand.   Altogether, the smuggling network moved, or tried  to move, at least $160 million worth of chips.   But here too, enforcement can help,  if it’s done right. When Washington   threatened to restrict AI chip shipments to  Malaysia, Malaysia started requiring permits   to export them. Chinese imports of servers from  Malaysia and Singapore then fell by about 80%.   But the biggest channel is renting.  And if you see China as a threat,   this one feels particularly ridiculous. You don’t need physical access to AI chips   to use them. You can rent time on them  in a data centre anywhere in the world.   US rules prevent NVIDIA from selling its best  chips to Chinese companies. But they don’t stop   Chinese companies from renting those same chips  in a data centre abroad. So that’s what they do.   The Chinese AI company Tencent has a deal  to rent top chips from the American company   Oracle. ByteDance runs a cluster of NVIDIA’s best  chips in Norway. But the majority of the computing   power being rented sits in Southeast  Asia, mostly Malaysia and Singapore.   Here’s what that looks like. In 2025, four Chinese  engineers flew from Beijing to Malaysia, where   they’d rented about 300 servers full of NVIDIA  chips. Sending that much data over the internet   could have taken months, so they carried it in  suitcases, each packed with 15 hard drives of   training data. The plan was to train their model  in Malaysia, and then just fly back with it.   Meanwhile, American companies don’t have enough  chips. Amazon runs one of the world’s biggest   cloud businesses, and they say they won’t have  enough computing power to meet customer demand   this year or next. So a chip that doesn’t  go to China doesn’t go to waste. Someone   else buys it — mostly American customers. And this is where, for me, the race argument   starts to fall apart. You’d expect the people  making it to want these channels closed. Instead,   some of its loudest voices have  pushed to sell China more chips.   NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has warned “China is just  nanoseconds behind the US.” He’s also said export   controls cost NVIDIA its Chinese market. His  solution is to sell China more NVIDIA chips, to   keep Chinese developers using American technology.  But notice how neatly that fits his business.   David Sacks said every month counts. But  as White House AI czar, he pushed to loosen   restrictions on NVIDIA’s sales abroad. The  New York Times found he held stakes in 449   AI-related companies while shaping AI policy. Sacks says ethics officials signed off. But his   ethics waivers were issued by the White House’s  own lawyers, a month after Trump fired the head of   the government’s independent ethics office. Either  way, I think the incentives are worth noticing.   Okay, but even with all those  chips, the numbers don’t add up.   On computing power alone, researchers  estimate China should be about 13 months   behind. So what’s making up that difference? The answer is something called “distillation.”   You ask a stronger AI model millions of questions.  You record its answers, and its reasoning. Then   you train your own model to imitate it. It’s like  copying a top student’s worked solutions. But   you don’t just get the answers. You also learn  how they think, for a fraction of the effort.   Chinese labs do this at an enormous scale. Anthropic says Alibaba alone exchanged more   than 151 million messages with Claude in  just three months. The Institute for Progress   estimated distillation closes roughly half the  gap between American models and Chinese ones.   That’s like giving Chinese AI  companies four times as many chips.   So why don’t American AI companies stop  the Chinese ones from copying? To do that,   companies have to catch huge numbers of fake  accounts. In one campaign, DeepSeek, Moonshot,   and MiniMax used roughly 24,000 of them. But it can be done. Anthropic says it cut   the data that copiers can harvest from  its models by between 90 and 99%.   The catch is that copiers just go wherever the  defences are weakest. Zhipu tried to copy the   hacking skills of Anthropic’s top public  model, got blocked, but then switched to   models with weaker safeguards. Its next  model was rated the most capable hacking   model anyone has ever released for free. And there’s an awkward incentive. Copiers   pay to use these models, just like any other  customer. So every company that blocks them   loses money to the ones that don’t. So China is buying, smuggling,   and renting American computing power, and  copying American frontier models. Does that   mean they’re losing the AI race? Ask China’s own AI leaders,   and they’re surprisingly frank: in the race to  build the smartest AI, yes, they’re behind.   At a conference in Beijing in January,  Lin Junyang, who was at that point a   technical lead on Alibaba’s Qwen models, put  China’s chance of overtaking top American AI   companies at less than 20% in the next three  to five years. And he called that “highly   optimistic.” His reason was computing power. On the same panel, Zhipu’s chief AI scientist,   Tang Jie, went further. He said “the gap may  in fact be widening,” because many of the US’s   best models aren’t public. But building the smartest   AI models is only one way to win at AI. Beijing seems to be running a different race   altogether: using it everywhere. Its goal isn’t to  make the best chatbot. It’s AI in every factory,   hospital, and government office. And in  that race, China has real advantages.   For one, it has power. AI data centres  need enormous amounts of electricity,   and in the US, that’s becoming a real problem.  American data centres could face a 44-gigawatt   shortfall by 2028. That’s like needing  to add another California to the US power   grid in just over a year from now. China does not have that problem.   It’s expected to add almost six times as much  generating capacity as the US over the next five   years. So right now, China’s bottleneck is chips.  Which means if China ever solves its chip problem,   it won’t hit the wall the US is running into.  It’ll already have the power to run them.   China also has factories and robots. Last year,  China installed about 354,000 industrial robots,   which is 59% of the world’s total. The  US installed about a tenth as many.   And in the first half of this year, 97% of  the humanoid robots sold anywhere in the   world were made by Chinese companies. It also  controls most of the supply chain behind them,   from the minerals to the batteries to the  powerful magnets that drive robot joints.   So the picture is more complicated than  one race with one finish line. In the   race the US is running — the one to build the  smartest AI — China is still behind. But again,   not by that much… which puts  the US in a tricky position.   I don’t love the US–China AI “race” framing.  Treating AI like an arms race is exactly the   kind of thinking that pushes everyone  to cut corners on safety. But there are   a few reasons to want a bigger gap. For one, it would help the US capture   more of AI’s economic gains. And it  would let the US shore up its cyber   defences before anyone else can attack them. But the reason I personally care about most is   breathing room. I’m extremely worried that  we’re building AI faster than we can make   it safe or secure. A bigger gap means time  to slow down: to test new models properly,   and hold back the ones that aren’t ready yet. And here’s the thing: the US might already   have that time. Six months is actually  a pretty long time in AI. And because so   much of China’s progress comes from  distillation — basically copying US   models — the real gap is bigger than it looks. Matt Sheehan, who studies Chinese AI policy,   compares China to a wakesurfer riding the wave  behind a boat. It keeps up partly because the   boat is doing a lot of the work. If the boat  slows down, the wave shrinks. China doesn’t   suddenly shoot ahead. It would then have to  rely on its own engine, which is much smaller.   So the US may already have time to slow down. But if it wanted to, how could the US widen   the gap even more? Mostly with  powers the government already has.   First, there’s renting, which lets Chinese  companies use huge numbers of American chips   abroad. Neither party has stopped it: Biden-era  regulators chose not to restrict it, and a later   attempt was scrapped by the Trump administration. But it’s very fixable. A bill to help restrict   renting has already passed the House, so now  it just needs to be passed by the Senate.   And regulators don’t even need to wait for  the bill. They could already require that   chips sold abroad can’t be rented out  to Chinese companies at scale — ideally   alongside a crackdown on smuggling, so  the demand doesn’t just go underground.   The government could also stop approving  sales of chips like the H200, and limit the   gaming cards being used for AI. And in the long run, the biggest   lever might be the older chipmaking  machines China still buys from ASML,   and the maintenance ASML provides for them. Some  analysts argue that cutting off both could lock   in the US advantage for at least a decade. Put together, the Institute for Progress   estimates these steps could add several  months to the US lead by the end of the year,   and maybe even double it. The exact number is  rough. But the direction is clear: the size of   the lead is in large part a policy choice. So why hasn’t the US done all this?   Partly, it’s incentives. NVIDIA wants the  sales, and copiers are paying customers.   But there’s also an argument on the other side  — the one David Sacks and Jensen Huang made:   cutting China off just pushes it to build its  own chips, and reduce its dependence on the US.   Now, Huang runs the company that would lose those  sales, so it is tempting to write him off. But   researchers with nothing to sell make versions  of the same argument. Analysts at the Center for   Strategic and International Studies concluded  that broad US controls have sped up China’s   push to stop relying on American technology. So  maybe if you cut China off, you give it every   reason to build its own technology instead. Once  it can, the US would lose that leverage for good.   There’s a second worry too: controls  make cooperation harder. Matt Sheehan   says Beijing’s first read of American AI policy  is that the US wants to hold China down. That   makes any deal between the two countries harder  to reach, including one to slow down together.   So should the US hold off on closing  these gaps? I don’t think so.   China was trying to build its own chips long  before the US export controls. Back in 2015,   its “Made in China 2025” plan set a  target of making 70% of its own chips.   Selling China chips doesn’t stop it building  its own. Remember when the US approved sales   of NVIDIA’s H200 this year, Beijing told its  companies to hold off, to protect China’s own   chip industry. So Beijing will build its own  chips either way. The question is whether it   also gets American chips in the meantime. Then there’s timing. Building a whole chip   industry from scratch takes years — maybe  even decades. ASML started working on its   most advanced machines in the 1990s. They  cost billions of dollars and took two decades,   and only entered mass production in 2019. If powerful AI is coming in the next five years,   as many experts in the industry believe, China’s  own chips won’t be ready in time. What matters   is how close its best models are now. And  right now, that depends a lot on American   chips and American models. But there’s one more risk,   and it could undermine the lead the US already  has — even if it does manage to widen the gap.   You might assume the most powerful AI models  in the world are guarded like nuclear secrets.   They are very much not. And that makes  two very precious things relatively   easy to steal if China wanted to. One is a model itself. An AI model,   at its core, is one very large file — so if you  steal that file, you’ve stolen the whole model.   The other is how a model was built: the  techniques and breakthroughs that make   each new model better than the last. Security experts rate how well AI   companies protect these on a scale  from 1 to 5. Level 5 means you could   stop the world’s most capable spy agencies. The best public estimates put top American   AI companies somewhere around a 2 or a 3.  An industry task force is working out how   companies could reach level 5 by 2028 or 2029.  But it would be entirely voluntary — nothing   would require them to do it. So a nuclear power plant has to   meet strict federal security rules, but  the companies building what might be the   most powerful technology in history don’t. And China is already going after American   AI secrets. In January, Linwei  Ding, a former Google engineer,   was convicted of stealing thousands of pages of  Google’s AI secrets while secretly working for   two Chinese tech companies. Those pages showed  how Google builds the supercomputers it uses   to train its AI — which is exactly the kind of  computing power China has struggled to build.   No theft of a top model has been publicly  confirmed yet. But the techniques behind   them are clearly a target. So how bad would it be if   these things were stolen? I’ll start with the model   itself. Once stolen, China gets everything  it can do, including the dangerous stuff.   Take hacking. In August, AI models helped  researchers find critical flaws in PHP,   software that runs on about 70% of the world’s  websites. The researchers tried to keep it quiet   while it was fixed. But in October, details  leaked, and governments rushed to pull websites   offline before hackers could use them. If China stole a model like that… they’d   basically have a cyberweapon  with unprecedented capabilities.   There’s also biology. Companies already  add safeguards because their models might   help someone make a bioweapon. A stolen  model comes without those safeguards.   Then there are breakthroughs. A stolen model  pretty quickly becomes obsolete. But stolen   breakthroughs in how to design or train AI  could help China build better models long   after they’ve stolen them. That could give China  a lasting boost, even with less computing power.   For me, that’s the scariest part, because  it could eat into the room the US has to   slow down. If the US slows down, China has to  make progress on their own, without copying,   and with far fewer chips. Stolen breakthroughs  could let it close the gap in a lasting way.   But unlike China’s chips, security  is entirely in the US’s hands.   And security at American AI companies  could be much, much better than it is   right now. It’s honestly kind of crazy that  it isn’t better already. But that’s fixable.   China buys, smuggles, and rents American chips. It  trains on answers from American models. And with   security as weak as it is, China could steal the  models themselves, or the techniques behind them.   All of which puts some serious holes  in the argument that the US can’t   slow down because China will catch up. So if you care about competing with China,   the first step isn’t going faster.  It’s to stop giving so much away.   In fact, slowing down might not be as costly as  it sounds. A researcher at Forethought estimates   that a top American company’s computing  edge could let it do research almost   twice as fast as its Chinese counterpart.  So the US could put some of that speed   into safety and security, and still keep pace. But a bigger lead only helps if the US actually   uses it to make models safer and more secure. What the US AI companies are doing right now is   terrifying. They don’t seem to be fully in control  of their own models, but they’re using them to   build the next generation of AIs anyway. I’m not certain about all of this. But I   am confident of one thing. If the race with  China is the reason the US can’t slow down,   it should at least be doing the things  that would actually keep it ahead.   Because right now, China  is renting American chips.

and MiniMax used roughly 24,000 of them. But it can be done. Anthropic says it cut
the data that copiers can harvest from  its models by between 90 and 99%.
The catch is that copiers just go wherever the  defences are weakest. Zhipu tried to copy the
hacking skills of Anthropic’s top public  model, got blocked, but then switched to
models with weaker safeguards. Its next  model was rated the most capable hacking
model anyone has ever released for free. And there’s an awkward incentive. Copiers
pay to use these models, just like any other  customer. So every company that blocks them
loses money to the ones that don’t. So China is buying, smuggling,
and renting American computing power, and  copying American frontier models. Does that
mean they’re losing the AI race? Ask China’s own AI leaders,
and they’re surprisingly frank: in the race to  build the smartest AI, yes, they’re behind.
At a conference in Beijing in January,  Lin Junyang, who was at that point a
technical lead on Alibaba’s Qwen models, put  China’s chance of overtaking top American AI
companies at less than 20% in the next three  to five years. And he called that “highly
optimistic.” His reason was computing power. On the same panel, Zhipu’s chief AI scientist,
Tang Jie, went further. He said “the gap may  in fact be widening,” because many of the US’s
best models aren’t public. But building the smartest
AI models is only one way to win at AI. Beijing seems to be running a different race
altogether: using it everywhere. Its goal isn’t to  make the best chatbot. It’s AI in every factory,
hospital, and government office. And in  that race, China has real advantages.
For one, it has power. AI data centres  need enormous amounts of electricity,
and in the US, that’s becoming a real problem.  American data centres could face a 44-gigawatt
shortfall by 2028. That’s like needing  to add another California to the US power
grid in just over a year from now. China does not have that problem.
It’s expected to add almost six times as much  generating capacity as the US over the next five
years. So right now, China’s bottleneck is chips.  Which means if China ever solves its chip problem,
it won’t hit the wall the US is running into.  It’ll already have the power to run them.
China also has factories and robots. Last year,  China installed about 354,000 industrial robots,
which is 59% of the world’s total. The  US installed about a tenth as many.
And in the first half of this year, 97% of  the humanoid robots sold anywhere in the
world were made by Chinese companies. It also  controls most of the supply chain behind them,
from the minerals to the batteries to the  powerful magnets that drive robot joints.
So the picture is more complicated than  one race with one finish line. In the
race the US is running — the one to build the  smartest AI — China is still behind. But again,
not by that much… which puts  the US in a tricky position.
I don’t love the US–China AI “race” framing.  Treating AI like an arms race is exactly the
kind of thinking that pushes everyone  to cut corners on safety. But there are
a few reasons to want a bigger gap. For one, it would help the US capture
more of AI’s economic gains. And it  would let the US shore up its cyber
defences before anyone else can attack them. But the reason I personally care about most is
breathing room. I’m extremely worried that  we’re building AI faster than we can make
it safe or secure. A bigger gap means time  to slow down: to test new models properly,
and hold back the ones that aren’t ready yet. And here’s the thing: the US might already
have that time. Six months is actually  a pretty long time in AI. And because so
much of China’s progress comes from  distillation — basically copying US
models — the real gap is bigger than it looks. Matt Sheehan, who studies Chinese AI policy,
compares China to a wakesurfer riding the wave  behind a boat. It keeps up partly because the
boat is doing a lot of the work. If the boat  slows down, the wave shrinks. China doesn’t
suddenly shoot ahead. It would then have to  rely on its own engine, which is much smaller.
So the US may already have time to slow down. But if it wanted to, how could the US widen
the gap even more? Mostly with  powers the government already has.
First, there’s renting, which lets Chinese  companies use huge numbers of American chips
abroad. Neither party has stopped it: Biden-era  regulators chose not to restrict it, and a later
attempt was scrapped by the Trump administration. But it’s very fixable. A bill to help restrict
renting has already passed the House, so now  it just needs to be passed by the Senate.
And regulators don’t even need to wait for  the bill. They could already require that
chips sold abroad can’t be rented out  to Chinese companies at scale — ideally
alongside a crackdown on smuggling, so  the demand doesn’t just go underground.
The government could also stop approving  sales of chips like the H200, and limit the
gaming cards being used for AI. And in the long run, the biggest
lever might be the older chipmaking  machines China still buys from ASML,
and the maintenance ASML provides for them. Some  analysts argue that cutting off both could lock
in the US advantage for at least a decade. Put together, the Institute for Progress
estimates these steps could add several  months to the US lead by the end of the year,
and maybe even double it. The exact number is  rough. But the direction is clear: the size of
the lead is in large part a policy choice. So why hasn’t the US done all this?
Partly, it’s incentives. NVIDIA wants the  sales, and copiers are paying customers.
But there’s also an argument on the other side  — the one David Sacks and Jensen Huang made:
cutting China off just pushes it to build its  own chips, and reduce its dependence on the US.
Now, Huang runs the company that would lose those  sales, so it is tempting to write him off. But
researchers with nothing to sell make versions  of the same argument. Analysts at the Center for
Strategic and International Studies concluded  that broad US controls have sped up China’s
push to stop relying on American technology. So  maybe if you cut China off, you give it every
reason to build its own technology instead. Once  it can, the US would lose that leverage for good.
There’s a second worry too: controls  make cooperation harder. Matt Sheehan
says Beijing’s first read of American AI policy  is that the US wants to hold China down. That
makes any deal between the two countries harder  to reach, including one to slow down together.
So should the US hold off on closing  these gaps? I don’t think so.
China was trying to build its own chips long  before the US export controls. Back in 2015,
its “Made in China 2025” plan set a  target of making 70% of its own chips.
Selling China chips doesn’t stop it building  its own. Remember when the US approved sales
of NVIDIA’s H200 this year, Beijing told its  companies to hold off, to protect China’s own
chip industry. So Beijing will build its own  chips either way. The question is whether it
also gets American chips in the meantime. Then there’s timing. Building a whole chip
industry from scratch takes years — maybe  even decades. ASML started working on its
most advanced machines in the 1990s. They  cost billions of dollars and took two decades,
and only entered mass production in 2019. If powerful AI is coming in the next five years,
as many experts in the industry believe, China’s  own chips won’t be ready in time. What matters
is how close its best models are now. And  right now, that depends a lot on American
chips and American models. But there’s one more risk,
and it could undermine the lead the US already  has — even if it does manage to widen the gap.
You might assume the most powerful AI models  in the world are guarded like nuclear secrets.
They are very much not. And that makes  two very precious things relatively
easy to steal if China wanted to. One is a model itself. An AI model,
at its core, is one very large file — so if you  steal that file, you’ve stolen the whole model.
The other is how a model was built: the  techniques and breakthroughs that make
each new model better than the last. Security experts rate how well AI
companies protect these on a scale  from 1 to 5. Level 5 means you could
stop the world’s most capable spy agencies. The best public estimates put top American
AI companies somewhere around a 2 or a 3.  An industry task force is working out how
companies could reach level 5 by 2028 or 2029.  But it would be entirely voluntary — nothing
would require them to do it. So a nuclear power plant has to
meet strict federal security rules, but  the companies building what might be the
most powerful technology in history don’t. And China is already going after American
AI secrets. In January, Linwei  Ding, a former Google engineer,
was convicted of stealing thousands of pages of  Google’s AI secrets while secretly working for
two Chinese tech companies. Those pages showed  how Google builds the supercomputers it uses
to train its AI — which is exactly the kind of  computing power China has struggled to build.
No theft of a top model has been publicly  confirmed yet. But the techniques behind
them are clearly a target. So how bad would it be if
these things were stolen? I’ll start with the model
itself. Once stolen, China gets everything  it can do, including the dangerous stuff.
Take hacking. In August, AI models helped  researchers find critical flaws in PHP,
software that runs on about 70% of the world’s  websites. The researchers tried to keep it quiet
while it was fixed. But in October, details  leaked, and governments rushed to pull websites
offline before hackers could use them. If China stole a model like that… they’d
basically have a cyberweapon  with unprecedented capabilities.
There’s also biology. Companies already  add safeguards because their models might
help someone make a bioweapon. A stolen  model comes without those safeguards.
Then there are breakthroughs. A stolen model  pretty quickly becomes obsolete. But stolen
breakthroughs in how to design or train AI  could help China build better models long
after they’ve stolen them. That could give China  a lasting boost, even with less computing power.
For me, that’s the scariest part, because  it could eat into the room the US has to
slow down. If the US slows down, China has to  make progress on their own, without copying,
and with far fewer chips. Stolen breakthroughs  could let it close the gap in a lasting way.
But unlike China’s chips, security  is entirely in the US’s hands.
And security at American AI companies  could be much, much better than it is
right now. It’s honestly kind of crazy that  it isn’t better already. But that’s fixable.
China buys, smuggles, and rents American chips. It  trains on answers from American models. And with
security as weak as it is, China could steal the  models themselves, or the techniques behind them.
All of which puts some serious holes  in the argument that the US can’t
slow down because China will catch up. So if you care about competing with China,
the first step isn’t going faster.  It’s to stop giving so much away.
In fact, slowing down might not be as costly as  it sounds. A researcher at Forethought estimates
that a top American company’s computing  edge could let it do research almost
twice as fast as its Chinese counterpart.  So the US could put some of that speed
into safety and security, and still keep pace. But a bigger lead only helps if the US actually
uses it to make models safer and more secure. What the US AI companies are doing right now is
terrifying. They don’t seem to be fully in control  of their own models, but they’re using them to
build the next generation of AIs anyway. I’m not certain about all of this. But I
am confident of one thing. If the race with  China is the reason the US can’t slow down,
it should at least be doing the things  that would actually keep it ahead.
Because right now, China  is renting American chips.
